UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                            Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                                     COMMENTS OF
                            PERSISTENCE ANALYTICS GROUP LLC

                                         I. INTRODUCTION
      Persistence Analytics Group LLC ("PAG") respectfully submits these comments concerning PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C.'s August 13, 2026 proposal to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service
("IRAS") and a Large Load Registry. PAG supports the core objectives of improving visibility into
large-load development, protecting system reliability, and creating a more disciplined basis for the
treatment of new large loads. PAG's comments are limited to an implementation-assurance question
that becomes increasingly important as PJM, Electric Distributors, state commissions, and other
authorized entities begin to rely on registry information for consequential planning and operational
decisions.
      PJM's proposal recognizes that the Large Load Registry cannot function merely as a collection of
reported megawatts. The filing would require information concerning in-service dates, peak load and
ramp schedules, telemetry, Bring Your Own New Capacity ("BYONC"), backup generation and
permitting limitations, contracts or service agreements, and points of interconnection. PJM also
proposes authority to review information, coordinate with Transmission Owners and Electric
Distributors regarding validity, request additional information, and update the registry periodically.
PJM Filing at 37-45; proposed RAA Schedule 11, section B.
      Most significantly, PJM states that reliance on the registry must reflect accurate and complete
information and that the registry is intended to become an accurate, complete, and reliable database
supporting decisions about the amount of New Large Load available to provide IRAS. PJM Filing at
43-45. PAG agrees. The Commission should recognize that the quality of the framework will depend
not only on whether information is submitted, but also on whether material assumptions remain
sufficiently supported when the information is relied upon.
       Accordingly, PAG recommends that the Commission, in accepting or otherwise acting on the
filing, recognize four implementation principles for PJM's development of the Large Load Registry and
related Manuals: (1) material load information should be accompanied by sufficient context to
distinguish projected or requested load from more mature load states; (2) execution-critical assumptions
should be subject to identifiable revalidation triggers; (3) information used to support IRAS load-
reduction capability should be decision-useful for the actual operating conditions in which that
capability may be called; and (4) authorized users should have sufficient provenance to understand
what supports a material registry input and when it was last materially validated.

   II. THE LARGE LOAD REGISTRY SHOULD BE TREATED AS A DECISION-GRADE
          EVIDENTIARY RECORD, NOT ONLY A REPORTING REPOSITORY
      PJM proposes a registry with considerably more information than a conventional interconnection
queue. Among other items, each Party would submit or cause to be submitted the Large Load's
description and location, in-service date for each increment of load, delivery points or points of
interconnection, peak-load quantity and ramp schedule, telemetry specifications, BYONC quantity and
ramp schedule, allocated RBP UCAP, backup generation including fuel type and relevant permitting

                                                   1
 limitations, and contracts or service agreements between the Large Load and the LSE. PJM Filing at
37-38; proposed RAA Schedule 11, section B.1(a).
      Those fields reflect an important reality: a headline megawatt value does not, by itself, describe
the maturity, timing, operational characteristics, or reliability implications of a large-load project. A 500
MW value may represent a development envelope, a requested service level, a studied quantity, a
contracted commitment, a phased construction plan, an energized load, or a persistent operating level.
Those states can have materially different implications for capacity planning, transmission planning,
cost allocation, IRAS eligibility, and state retail treatment.
      PAG therefore recommends that implementation of the registry preserve enough context for
authorized users to understand the status represented by a material MW figure. This need not require
PJM to adopt a new public scoring system or to disclose commercially sensitive information. It can be
accomplished through clear definitions, dated status fields, source attribution, and structured
information about the stage to which the reported quantity relates.
      The objective is straightforward: information should be decision-grade for the decision being
made. A quantity suitable for early planning visibility may not be sufficient for an irreversible capital
commitment or an operational baseline. Recognizing that distinction would improve the usefulness of
the registry without slowing the interconnection of projects that have demonstrated sufficient maturity.

    III. MATERIAL ASSUMPTIONS SHOULD HAVE IDENTIFIABLE REVALIDATION
                                TRIGGERS
      PJM expressly proposes that each Party promptly inform the Office of the Interconnection of any
change in required registry information concerning a Large Load. Proposed RAA Schedule 11, section
B.2; PJM Filing at 43-44. That is an important foundation. PAG recommends that PJM's
implementation guidance make the concept operational by identifying categories of material change
that should trigger revalidation of affected assumptions.
      Examples can include a material change in the expected in-service date or ramp schedule; a
change in the customer or contractual commitment underlying the load; a change in the quantity,
timing, or status of BYONC; a change in backup-generation capability, fuel availability, or relevant
permitting limitations; a material change in points of interconnection or service configuration; or a
change that affects the facility's claimed ability to reduce load under IRAS.
        The purpose of revalidation is not to require continuous resubmission of unchanged information.
It is to prevent an assumption that was reasonable at one point in project development from remaining
embedded in planning or operational treatment after the conditions supporting it have materially
changed.
      This distinction is particularly important for projects developed in phases. PJM recognizes the
importance of in-service dates for each increment of load and of ramp schedules. PJM Filing at 38-40.
A phased project can change customer mix, construction sequence, equipment strategy, generation
arrangements, or energization timing while retaining the same ultimate development capacity. The
registry should allow those changes to be reflected before other entities continue relying on an outdated
implementation assumption.

 IV. IRAS RELIES ON OPERATIONAL CAPABILITY, SO CLAIMED LOAD REDUCTION
       SHOULD BE SUPPORTED BY OPERATIONALLY RELEVANT EVIDENCE
     IRAS is designed to allow certain New Large Loads to interconnect without sufficient new
capacity on the condition that they may be required to reduce load or switch to onsite backup resources
under specified emergency conditions. PJM Filing at 39-40, 74-100. The proposed registry accordingly

                                                     2
 includes telemetry specifications and backup generation, including fuel type and relevant permitting
limitations. PJM Filing at 37-38.
      That architecture makes operational capability a consequential assumption. A stated ability to
reduce 100 MW is not identical to a demonstrated ability to produce that reduction under the timing,
control, telemetry, fuel, permitting, and restoration conditions relevant to an IRAS event. The same
applies where onsite generation is part of the expected response.
       PAG does not suggest that every Large Load must be subjected to a single standardized physical
test. Facilities differ materially, and PJM and state authorities retain the appropriate operational and
regulatory roles. PAG instead recommends that the Commission recognize a principle of evidence
proportionality: where PJM or an Electric Distributor relies on a claimed operational capability to
protect reliability, the evidence supporting that capability should be commensurate with the
consequence of non-performance.
       At a minimum, the implementation framework should allow the relevant parties to understand the
quantity expected to be reduced, the mechanism by which reduction is expected to occur, telemetry or
visibility needed to confirm performance, material constraints on backup generation, and circumstances
that would require the capability to be revalidated. This would complement, rather than replace,
existing PJM emergency procedures and state-approved load-reduction plans.

   V. BYONC SHOWS WHY REPORTED ARRANGEMENTS AND DURABLE CAPACITY
                       SHOULD REMAIN DISTINCT
      PJM proposes BYONC as a pathway for New Large Loads to facilitate new capacity and reduce
the quantity of load subject to IRAS. The filing includes gating criteria intended to ensure that BYONC
represents genuinely new capacity rather than repackaged existing capacity, and it proposes
participation requirements designed to ensure that the capacity benefit is real and lasting. PJM Filing at
50-59.
       PAG supports the distinction embodied in those provisions. An announced generation project, a
bilateral arrangement, an interconnection milestone, an accredited Capacity Resource, and capacity that
remains available through the period on which the system relies are related but not interchangeable
facts. The registry and associated implementation processes should preserve that distinction.
      Where a New Large Load receives treatment based on a BYONC arrangement, authorized users
should be able to determine the relevant quantity, timing, status, and material changes affecting the
arrangement. PJM already proposes to collect BYONC quantity and ramp schedule and to associate
BYONC resources with Large Loads. PJM Filing at 37-43. PAG recommends that revalidation of
material changes be carried through to any registry or operational determination that depends on the
arrangement.

         VI. STATE COMMISSIONS AND ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTORS WILL NEED
         INFORMATION THAT IS RELIABLE FOR THEIR DISTINCT DECISIONS
      PJM's proposal expressly recognizes a significant state role. Electric Distributors would
coordinate, as appropriate, with relevant states or Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities,
LSEs, and customers to support transparent, effective, and orderly deployment of IRAS. PJM Filing at
27-28. The filing further explains that Electric Distributors, consistent with state programs, identify
which loads to reduce in response to a PJM directive, and that state-approved contracts and load-
reduction plans govern that implementation. PJM Filing at 85-100.




                                                    3
       The proposed registry may also be made available, subject to confidentiality protections, to
Authorized Commissions, Transmission Owners, Electric Distributors, LSEs, the Market Monitoring
Unit, and the Commission. PJM Filing at 42-44.
      These authorized users will not necessarily rely on the same field for the same purpose. A state
commission may be considering retail rate treatment or cost responsibility. An Electric Distributor may
be preparing an operational load-reduction plan. A Transmission Owner may be considering system
impacts. PJM may be establishing an IRAS baseline. The registry will be most valuable if a user can
understand both the reported value and the evidentiary context relevant to the decision at hand.
      PAG therefore recommends that PJM's implementation work preserve data provenance and
validation status for material fields where feasible. This can include the reporting entity, effective date,
last material update, and whether the field is based on a contract, utility study, operational
measurement, permit, accredited capacity status, customer representation, or another identified source
category. Such provenance can be protected under the same confidentiality framework that PJM
proposes for commercially sensitive information.

 VII. THESE PRINCIPLES CAN IMPROVE RELIABILITY WITHOUT CREATING A NEW
                             APPROVAL LAYER
      PAG's recommendations are intended to support PJM's proposed framework, not to create a
parallel interconnection process. The Commission need not require a new approval gate for every
registry field. Nor should an independent assurance concept displace the technical, legal, regulatory, or
operational responsibilities assigned to PJM, Transmission Owners, Electric Distributors, LSEs, Large
Loads, state commissions, or FERC.
      The narrower point is that institutional reliance should be matched to evidentiary maturity. As the
consequences of reliance increase, the importance of accurate status, provenance, and revalidation also
increases. PJM's filing already contains the core building blocks: structured information, validation
authority, periodic updating, prompt reporting of changes, confidentiality safeguards, and an explicit
requirement that the registry provide an accurate and reliable basis for IRAS.
       Implementation guidance can build on those elements without prescribing a proprietary
methodology. Clear status definitions, material-change triggers, source categories, and operationally
relevant evidence expectations would make the registry more useful to all authorized users and reduce
the risk that an outdated or insufficiently supported assumption becomes an operational baseline.

                                          VIII. CONCLUSION
      PAG supports PJM's effort to establish a Large Load Registry and an interim framework that
better aligns large-load integration with resource adequacy and ratepayer protection. The proposal
correctly recognizes that reliable implementation depends on more than collecting a headline MW
value.
       PAG respectfully recommends that the Commission recognize, in its consideration of the filing,
that: (1) material large-load information should carry sufficient context to distinguish planning-stage
projections from more mature implementation states; (2) execution-critical assumptions should be
subject to identifiable revalidation triggers; (3) claimed IRAS load-reduction or onsite-backup
capability should be supported by evidence appropriate to the operational consequence; and (4)
authorized users should have sufficient provenance to understand what supports a material registry
input and when that information was last materially validated.
     These principles would strengthen the reliability of the Large Load Registry while preserving
PJM's flexibility to develop detailed implementation provisions through its Manuals and stakeholder

                                                      4
 processes. They would also help state commissions and Electric Distributors use the registry for their
distinct responsibilities without treating all reported information as equally mature or equally reliable
for every decision.


Respectfully submitted,
Neil P. Osnato
Founder
